frontier.hypothesis: The last delay-slot divergence (emitted 45-47) closes iff $v0 is live at the entry of jump_insn 78's TARGET block (the `var_s1 = 0; goto block_15;` block at code_label 87). Target's compile must have that bit set; ours does not (oppregs = 0x20000380).
frontier.mechanism: fill_slots_from_thread's steal_delay_list_from_fallthrough on insn 78 is refused only by `insn_sets_resource_p (trial, &opposite_needed)`; opposite_needed here is the EXACT flow live-in of the beq's target block (find_basic_block resolves it cleanly from barrier 85 - not the -1 conservative fallback), so the axis is which registers flow believes are live entering that block, or alternatively making find_basic_block fail to resolve it (which forces the all-live conservative answer and refuses the steal).
frontier.next_probe: Two cheap, disjoint attacks. (i) LIVENESS: find a semantics-preserving spelling that makes $v0 live-in at the `var_s1 = 0; goto block_15;` block - e.g. merging that block with the `temp_v1 == 0x13` path's own `var_s1 = 0;` (insn 98 at code_label 95) so the beq targets a block with a different live-in, or routing block_15's first computation through a value already resident in $v0. (ii) BLOCK RESOLUTION: make the label after barrier 85 not be a basic_block_head so find_basic_block returns -1 (all-live => steal refused). Instrument with `bash tmp/grind/func_800283D0/s23/dbr.sh <tag>` and read the `thr insn=78 ... oppregs=` word; if bit 0x4 sets, the two points close. Do NOT re-run Q1/Q2-style relocations of the `return 1;` block (10 / 215 and 8 / 216).

frontier.hypothesis: The two commutative `addu` operand orders (emitted 96 and 161) are decided after fold, by the same allocation/emission choice, and will move together or not at all.
frontier.mechanism: Both source-order spellings are byte-neutral (s3 `both-operand-orders-neutral-11.c`, s22 `s22-temp-s3-addend-order-swap-neutral-6.c`, F2 on the 6-floor chassis), so GCC canonicalises the PLUS before RA and the emitted order reflects which pseudo the addend lives in, not the source. Both sites have the same shape: ours puts the long-lived register first, target puts the freshly computed one first.
frontier.next_probe: This is a solver/forensics question, not a structural one: read the .combine and .greg dumps for the two PLUS insns on the 4-floor chassis and determine whether the operand order is fixed at expand (RTL operand slots) or flipped later by regmove/reload. If it is fixed at expand, the only remaining lever is a different TREE (not a different operand order) for `arg0 + temp_a1_2 * 2` - e.g. an intermediate whose pseudo is born later. Cost is one dump.

frontier.hypothesis: The zero-cost target-thread-steal device that closed cluster B may apply to other blocks in this function whose $v0/$v1 writes sit before their own branch.
frontier.mechanism: The general rule proven this session: a value written BEFORE a branch and stolen backward by fill_simple poisons every earlier branch whose mark_target_live_regs walk passes the update_block marker; the same value written as the head of that branch's TARGET thread is stolen with INSN_FROM_TARGET_P and poisons nothing. Any block with that shape is a candidate.
